lesson.title: The Ingredients Inside a Non-Sinusoidal Wave
lesson.summary: Any periodic non-sinusoidal waveform can be broken into a sum of pure sine and cosine waves at the fundamental frequency and its integer multiples, and the harmonic content is simply the list of which of those multiples show up and how large each one is.
lesson.body:
A resistor, a filter, or an amplifier does not know or care that a signal is supposed to be a clean sine wave. In real circuits you constantly encounter waveforms that are periodic but not sinusoidal: the square wave out of a digital gate, the sawtooth in a sweep generator, the clipped output of an overdriven amplifier, the pulse train from a switch. The Fourier series is the tool that lets you treat any of these, as long as they repeat with period T, as a sum of a constant term plus sinusoids at the fundamental frequency f0 = 1/T and at every integer multiple of it: 2f0, 3f0, 4f0, and so on. Those multiples are the harmonics you met as a prerequisite concept, and the harmonic content of a waveform is the specific answer to two questions at once: which harmonics are actually present, and how big is each one.

Formally, the Fourier series writes a periodic function as f(t) = a0 + the sum over n = 1, 2, 3, ... of [an cos(n omega0 t) + bn sin(n omega0 t)], where omega0 = 2 pi f0 is the fundamental angular frequency. The coefficients an and bn are found by integrating the waveform against cosines and sines over one period. Harmonic content means looking at this list of coefficients and reading off a fingerprint: maybe only odd n are nonzero, maybe the amplitudes fall off quickly, maybe there is a strong third harmonic and almost nothing else. Two waveforms can share the same fundamental frequency and peak voltage and still sound, or behave, completely differently because their harmonic content differs.

Here is a fully worked example. Take an ideal square wave of peak amplitude A that equals +A for the first half of each period and -A for the second half. Setting up the wave so it is centered at zero (A for 0 < t < T/2, -A for -T/2 < t < 0), direct integration gives bn = 4A / (n pi) for every odd n, and bn = 0 for every even n; every an, including a0, is zero (you will see exactly why when symmetry is covered in the next few chapters). So the harmonic content of a 10 V peak, 1 kHz square wave is: fundamental at 1 kHz with amplitude 4(10)/pi = 12.73 V, third harmonic at 3 kHz with amplitude 12.73/3 = 4.24 V, fifth harmonic at 5 kHz with amplitude 12.73/5 = 2.55 V, seventh harmonic at 7 kHz with amplitude 12.73/7 = 1.82 V, and nothing at all at 2 kHz, 4 kHz, or 6 kHz. Notice the pattern: only odd harmonics appear, and their amplitudes shrink as 1/n.

This is exactly why a square wave sounds harsh compared to a sine wave of the same frequency: it is not one tone but a whole ladder of tones stacked on top of the fundamental, and it is why engineers designing switching power supplies or digital clock lines have to worry about harmonic content radiating or coupling into nearby circuits at 3x, 5x, 7x the clock frequency, not just at the clock frequency itself. Harmonic content is the raw list of numbers; the next two chapters turn that list into pictures you can read at a glance.
